models.name: Qwen 3.8 Flash Next 125B (Unsloth 3-bit)
models.rel_note: No release date found; it was already on benchlm.ai's Oct 29 ranking. Unsloth's Dynamic v3.1 files are dated Nov 4.
models.notes: A 125B mixture-of-experts model that uses about 6B parameters per token (plus a 51B lookup table and a 4B prediction head, about 180B in all). This is Unsloth's 3-bit file (89.5 GB); their other files run from 66 GB (1-bit) to 111 GB (4-bit). Reading it from Ollama needs a recent Ollama that knows this architecture; Ollama's own library tag is a 105 GB Apple-only MLX build. Quantizing costs accuracy: Unsloth reports the 3-bit file matches the full model's top answer 88% of the time (its 1-bit file 80%, 4-bit 92%), which measures similarity to the full model, not task scores. The 15% accuracy gain Unsloth claims over other quantizers is its own claim and unverified. Qwen's own full-precision claims: 58.7 on DeepSWE 1.1, 62.5 on SWE-bench Pro. benchlm.ai scores the full model 54.06 on Nov 13, tied with Qwen3.8 27B (55.69 on Nov 10; 56.12 on Nov 5). The license needs a separate commercial license for hosted AI services built on it. File size excludes the context cache, so plan for 10 to 20 GB more. Ollama 0.40.16 (Nov 9) says it now uses about 27 GiB less memory on Apple silicon (that is the Apple-only MLX build, not this file).

tasks.about: Per task, models are listed best-first by quality, regardless of whether they fit a given machine. The page walks the list and picks the best one that runs well on the selected machine. The order is editorial judgment informed by the sources in models.json (benchmark numbers are quoted in 'why' only where a source gave one), not a benchmark ranking. Reorder freely. {tag} and {companion_tag} in steps are replaced with the chosen model's Ollama tag.

comparisons.title: Not sure which coding option you want?

rows.label: What it does
rows.a: Suggests the next few lines as you type, answers questions about the code in front of you, and makes small edits you approve.
rows.b: You describe a job in plain words. It reads your project, edits several files, can run commands, and shows you the changes.

rows.label: Who is driving
rows.a: You. It is an assistant at your elbow.
rows.b: The AI. You review what it did afterwards.

rows.label: Example
rows.a: Type a function name, press Tab to accept the finished body. Select code and ask "why does this crash?"
rows.b: "Add a dark mode setting and update the tests."

rows.label: How it feels
rows.a: Instant. Suggestions have to appear while you are still typing.
rows.b: You wait, sometimes minutes, then review the result.

rows.label: What matters most in a model
rows.a: Speed. A small fast model beats a big slow one.
rows.b: Smarts and reliable tool use. A bigger, slower model is worth the wait.

rows.label: Pick this if
rows.a: You write most of the code yourself and want a fast helper.
rows.b: You want to hand off whole tasks and are happy to review the results.

comparisons.note: Many people use both: a small fast model for typing help, and a bigger one for agent jobs. The page picks the right model for each.

comparisons.title: Chat, reasoning or documents: which one?

rows.label: What it does
vals: Answers questions, drafts and edits text, summarizes.
Works through multi-step problems: math, logic, planning, weighing options against constraints.
Finds the right passages in your own files and answers from them.

rows.label: How it feels
vals: Quick replies, faster than you can read.
The model thinks first, so replies are slower and longer.

rows.label: Example
vals: "Rewrite this email so it sounds friendlier."
"Schedule these meetings so nobody has a conflict."
"What does the contract say about termination?" over a folder of PDFs.

rows.label: Speed target
vals: About 7 words per second (10 tokens/s) or faster.
Same target, but replies are long, so expect to wait.
Same target, plus a second small model for searching.

rows.label: Pick this if

The problem is hard and you will wait for a better answer.

comparisons.note: They can use the same model. The difference is how you use it: reasoning adds thinking time, and documents add a search step over your files.

common_steps.title: Install Ollama
common_steps.body: Download the Windows installer from ollama.com/download and run it. Ollama runs in the background and serves models on this computer only (http://localhost:11434).

mac.body: Download Ollama for macOS from ollama.com/download, drag it to Applications and open it once. It runs from the menu bar and serves models on this computer only (http://localhost:11434).

linux.body: Run the official install script from ollama.com/download. Ollama then runs as a background service and serves models on this computer only (http://localhost:11434).

common_steps.title: Download and try the model
common_steps.body: Open a terminal (PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on Mac and Linux) and run this. The first run downloads the model, then you can chat with it right there. Type /bye to exit.

common_steps.title: Check it is really using your GPU
common_steps.cpu_body: While the model is loaded, run this in a second terminal. This machine has no usable GPU, so PROCESSOR will say 100% CPU, which is expected. Look at the SIZE and CONTEXT columns to see how much memory the model is using.
common_steps.body: While the model is loaded, run this in a second terminal and look at the PROCESSOR column. 100% GPU is ideal. A split such as 40%/60% CPU/GPU means part of the model spilled into system RAM, which is slower.

common_steps.title: Raise the context length only if you need it
common_steps.body: Ollama's default context is 4096 tokens, which is short for long documents or code. The quickest fix is to type /set parameter num_ctx 8192 inside a chat. To make it permanent, set a user environment variable named OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH (for example 8192) and restart Ollama. More context uses more memory, and on a small GPU it can push the model into CPU offload, so re-check ollama ps afterwards.

mac.body: Ollama's default context is 4096 tokens, which is short for long documents or code. The quickest fix is to type /set parameter num_ctx 8192 inside a chat. To make it permanent, run the command below, then quit and reopen Ollama. More context uses more memory, so re-check ollama ps afterwards.

linux.body: Ollama's default context is 4096 tokens, which is short for long documents or code. The quickest fix is to type /set parameter num_ctx 8192 inside a chat. To make it permanent, run the command below, add the two lines [Service] and Environment="OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=8192" in the editor that opens, save, then restart the service with sudo systemctl restart ollama. More context uses more memory, so re-check ollama ps afterwards.

tasks.label: Code help as I type
tasks.blurb: A fast assistant inside your editor. It suggests the next lines as you type, explains or fixes the code you select, and makes small edits you approve. You stay in charge and write most of the code yourself. This needs a code editor that can add extensions: the setup below uses Continue, which works in VS Code and JetBrains editors (IntelliJ, PyCharm and others). If you do not use one of those, pick the coding agent or chat instead.
tasks.plain_rule: Code suggestions only help if they keep up with your typing, so speed matters more than size here.
tasks.example: Examples: grey suggestions appear as you type and you press Tab to accept one; you select a function and ask "what does this do?" or "fix this error". It works on the file in front of you and answers in a second or two.

ranked.why: Continue's docs recommend Qwen2.5-Coder 7B for typing help. Models of 10B or less are enough; bigger ones are slower without a significant gain.
Also recommended by Continue's docs, and the fastest choice. Use this on computers without a graphics card.
Built for completing code in the middle of a file, but slow at this size, and its license (Mistral Non-Production) forbids commercial use.

steps.title: Give it the right context
steps.body: Feed the model the current file and the few files it directly depends on, not the whole project. Small models do better with less, focused context.

tips: Autocomplete needs speed more than size, so this task wants a model that runs at 30+ tokens per second. Bigger models are better at hard problems: use the agent task below for those.

Models removed from this list: Phi-4 mini and DeepSeek-Coder-V2 were not confirmed to work for as-you-type suggestions. Continue's docs say thinking models and general chat models are a poor fit; a 'thinking' model only works with thinking switched off.
Ollama unloads an idle model after 5 minutes, so the first suggestion after a break can lag. A secondary source suggests setting OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 to keep it loaded.

tasks.label: Coding agent (hand off a whole job)
tasks.blurb: You describe a job in plain words, like "add a login page and update the tests". The AI reads your project, edits several files, can run commands, and shows you the changes to review. Slower, but it can finish bigger jobs while you do something else.
tasks.plain_rule: A coding agent can pause between steps, so a bigger, smarter model that is a little slower is the right trade.
tasks.example: Example: you type "add a settings page and update the tests". The AI reads your project, edits several files, runs commands, and shows you the changes to review. It can take a minute or more.

ranked.why: Newer than Qwen 3.6 27B at the same size. Qwen's own model card (not independently re-run) reports SWE-bench Pro 61.7 vs 53.5 and Terminal Bench 2.1 73.0 vs 63.4 for 3.6. Needs Ollama 0.32.12 or newer.
77.2% on SWE-bench Verified and 83.9 on LiveCodeBench in one benchmark roundup, the best numbers among models that run at home.
Largest gpt-oss. No benchmark number from my sources, but the 20B version in the same family scored 60.7% on SWE-bench Verified.
60.7% on SWE-bench Verified in one source; built for agentic coding and tool use; runs in about 16 GB of memory.
Coding-specific mixture-of-experts model with tool calling. Ollama lists integrations with several coding agents.
Built for multi-file agentic edits; 46.8% on SWE-bench Verified in one source.
ranked.tip: This is the older Devstral. Mistral also has a newer Devstral Small 2: check ollama.com/library/devstral.

ranked.why: Solid smaller coder when the bigger agents do not fit.
Smallest sensible option for light agent work.

steps.title: Use a longer context
steps.body: Agent tools send a lot of text, so a 4096-token context will not be enough. Start at 16K or more (step 4) and re-check ollama ps, because a longer context needs more memory.

tips: Agent models need to support tool calling. Check that the model's page on ollama.com/library shows the 'tools' tag.

Which tool? Hermes, opencode, Goose and Aider run in a terminal and work on a whole project folder. Cline does the same job inside VS Code. They all connect to the same Ollama address, so you can try each with the same model.

tasks.label: Hard reasoning, math & analysis
tasks.blurb: Multi-step problems, planning, checking constraints. Models think before answering, so replies are slower and longer.
tasks.plain_rule: Hard problems reward the smartest model that still answers at a comfortable pace.
tasks.example: Examples: a tricky math or logic puzzle, weighing several options against a list of constraints, planning a schedule with conflicts.

ranked.why: Largest reasoning-capable open model in this list.
Top overall score among the open models in one roundup.
Mistral's reasoning model. One source suggests capping context near 40K.
Reasoning model that fits in about 16 GB.
Distilled reasoning model; one source suggests it for multi-step analysis and constraint checking.
Reasoning-capable and small enough for a 6 GB GPU.

tips: Reasoning models write out their thinking first, so the first words can take a while to appear. That is normal.

phone_ranked.why: Thinks before answering by default, and is small enough to be quick. Editorial pick: no benchmark compares these on this phone.
Also has an extended thinking mode, and is bigger, so slower.
A stronger reasoner, but not in the app's list: add it from Hugging Face.

tasks.label: Ask questions about my documents
tasks.blurb: Search and answer from your own notes, PDFs and files. Uses two models: a small one to find the right passages, and a chat model to answer.
tasks.plain_rule: Answering from your documents needs a smart model that can read long text without crawling.
tasks.example: Examples: asking "what does the contract say about termination?" over a folder of PDFs, or searching your own notes by meaning instead of exact words.

ranked.why: Strong all-rounder with a 256K context window.
256K context window.
128K context and fits in about 16 GB.
256K context; the KV cache barely grows with long context, so long documents are cheap.
Best quality per unit of memory among the small embedding models, per one source.
Good if your documents are in several languages.
The easiest general English option on modest hardware.
Tiny and CPU-friendly but the least accurate.

steps.title: Download the search model too
steps.body: This small model turns your documents into searchable vectors.

tips: Retrieval (searching your own files) usually beats fine-tuning a model on them, and it stays current as your files change.

tasks.label: Describe images & read screenshots
tasks.blurb: Ask questions about photos, screenshots, charts and scanned pages.
tasks.plain_rule: Reading images needs a model built to see, and bigger ones read screenshots and charts more accurately.
tasks.example: Examples: "What is wrong in this screenshot?", "Read the numbers off this chart", "Describe this photo".

ranked.why: Highest vision benchmarks at this size tier, per one source.
Top current Qwen model; Ollama lists image input.
Mixture-of-experts Qwen with image input.
Fast multimodal mixture-of-experts model.
Strong at OCR, charts and math from images.
Multimodal and small.
The best-supported small vision model in Ollama.
Fits a 6 GB GPU with little headroom, but it is not in Ollama.
Lowest-memory vision model in Ollama.

steps.title: Ask about an image from the terminal
steps.body: In an ollama run session, type your question followed by the full path to the image file. On Windows a path looks like C:\Users\you\Pictures\screenshot.png. For example:

tips: For pure text extraction from scanned documents, a dedicated OCR model such as PaddleOCR-VL (0.9B, runs on CPU, not available in Ollama) can beat a general vision model.

tasks.label: Automations & tool calling
tasks.blurb: Workflows and scripts where the model must call tools, return clean JSON, or follow strict instructions (n8n, custom scripts).
tasks.plain_rule: Automations need a model that follows instructions and calls tools reliably, and they can run a bit slower because nobody is waiting on them.
tasks.example: Examples: an n8n workflow that reads an email and returns clean JSON, or a script that lets the model decide which tool to call.

ranked.why: Largest open model built for tool use in this list.
Strong agentic results in the benchmark roundup.
Memory-efficient, designed for agentic work and tool use.
Reliable tool calling per the Ollama library listings.
Supports tool calling; code-focused.
Built for tools and clean JSON output; Apache 2.0.
Tiny enterprise model made for tool calling; Apache 2.0.
Handles tool calling in a very small package.

steps.title: Connect your tool to Ollama
steps.body: In n8n, add an Ollama Chat Model node and set the base URL to http://localhost:11434. In your own scripts, call the same address. Pick a model with the 'tools' tag on ollama.com/library.

steps.title: If the tool runs on another machine
steps.body: Ollama only listens on this computer by default. To reach it from elsewhere, set the OLLAMA_HOST environment variable to 0.0.0.0:11434 (the same way as the context-length setting above: a user environment variable on Windows, launchctl setenv on Mac, a systemd override on Linux) and restart Ollama. Only do this on a network you trust: there is no password.

tips: For automations, reliability matters more than size. Test your real prompt 10 times before trusting it.

tasks.label: Financial analysis (filings, statements, numbers)
tasks.blurb: Read reports, statements and filings, pull out the figures, and reason about them. Accuracy matters more than speed here, and the model should never be trusted to do the arithmetic itself.
tasks.plain_rule: Financial work rewards the most accurate model you can run, and it still needs its numbers checked.
tasks.example: Examples: pulling revenue and margins out of a 10-K, comparing two years of statements, checking a budget for gaps, sorting transactions into categories. This helps you analyze documents; it is not investment advice.

ranked.why: The top single-GPU open model on the Finance Agent v2 table at benchlm.ai (48.6% at its highest reasoning setting, data verified 2026-10-29). Better-scoring open models there need multi-GPU servers. In November the benchmark moved to a v2.1 whose scores are not comparable, and a v2.1 score for this model was not found.

The largest model here that fits one 80 GB GPU or a large-RAM machine. An independent small test of extracting figures from 10-Ks used it: 75% exact before checking, 84% after (5 test filings, so rough).
The same family in about 16 GB. No finance score was found for it, so this ranking is editorial.
The previous Qwen 27B. No finance score found; ranked below its successor.
256K context for long filings. No finance score found.
IBM's page lists extraction, classification, RAG and structured JSON output among its uses (the maker's description, not a finance test).
256K context in a small size. No finance score found.
Small enough for a 6 GB GPU, but expect more mistakes: on financial tables the gap between strong and small models was large in published tests.
Best quality per unit of memory among the small embedding models, per one source.
Good if your documents are in several languages.
The easiest general English option on modest hardware.
Tiny and CPU-friendly but the least accurate.

steps.title: Download the search model too
steps.body: This small model finds the right passages in long filings so the chat model reads only those.

steps.title: Give it clean, labeled text
steps.body: Flattened tables confuse models. Keep each table's rows and columns, and state the units and conventions up front (thousands or millions, how negatives are shown, GAAP or IFRS, fiscal year end). Models cannot reliably guess units from context. Start your chat with something like this:
steps.cmd: Units: all figures are in US dollars, in thousands. Negatives are in parentheses. Fiscal year ends Dec 31. Use only the text I give you. If a figure is not in the text, say "not found".

steps.title: Make it quote its source for every number
steps.body: Ask for the exact line and page behind each figure. A figure with no quote is a guess. Errors are much easier to catch when each one is tied to a line you can look up.
steps.cmd: For every figure, give: the value, the exact line of text it came from, and the page. Return a table.

steps.title: Have it write the math, not do it
steps.body: Language models slip on multi-step arithmetic. In published tests on financial tables, asking for a small program and running it beat having the model calculate in words for the stronger models, and calculation mistakes were roughly a fifth to a quarter of all errors. So ask for code, run it yourself, and read the result.
steps.cmd: Do not calculate in your head. Write a short Python script that computes the growth rate and operating margin from these figures, and show me the script and its output.

steps.title: Check the figures against the source
steps.body: In one test, most wrong extractions quoted a real line but changed a digit or dropped a decimal. Compare each extracted number with its quoted line (a spreadsheet formula or a ten-line script works), and check that subtotals, margins and growth rates reconcile with the lines they come from.
steps.cmd: List each figure next to the source line. Then check that the subtotals add up to the totals, and tell me every place they do not.

steps.title: Treat modeling and judgement as a draft
steps.body: Models do far better at finding and summarizing figures than at building a financial model or judging a valuation: on the Finance Agent v2 benchmark, leaders scored above 70% on retrieval and summarization but about 35% on financial modeling. Use the output as a first pass and review the assumptions yourself.

tips: Run the same question twice with the thinking setting on and off, and compare the numbers. If they differ, go to the source.

For recurring work (say monthly statements), keep a short rules file with your units, definitions and the format you want, and load it each session. See the memory and context file tips under the tool.
Sorting transactions into categories is a simpler job than analysis, and small models do it well. Check a random sample of the results by hand.
Your documents stay on your machine with a local model. That is the main reason to use one for finance, and it is worth the loss in capability.

Evaluating LLMs' mathematical reasoning in financial documents (ACL 2024 Findings)
finextract: LLM hallucinations extracting figures from 10-Ks
Processing tabular financial data with LLMs (Daloopa, a vendor blog)

clients.about: Tools that talk to the model once Ollama is running. They are interchangeable: every one connects to the same local Ollama address. {tag} and {ctx} are filled in from the recommendation. Steps come from each tool's own docs (see 'docs'), checked on the date shown.

clients.name: Hermes Agent
clients.kind: Coding and general agent (terminal) from Nous Research
clients.blurb: A terminal agent that can edit files, run commands and browse. It can run on a different machine from the model (for example on a small server with the model served from a stronger computer).

steps.title: Install it
steps.body: Windows and Mac also have a desktop installer on the Hermes website. After installing, reload your terminal. This is the command-line install for Linux, Mac and WSL2.

windows.body: Run this in PowerShell. The Hermes website also has a desktop installer. After installing, reopen your terminal.

steps.title: Make a 64K-context copy of the model
steps.body: Hermes needs a model with at least 64,000 tokens of context, and Ollama's default is only 2048 to 4096. Hermes' own guide fixes this by making a copy of the model with a bigger context. First create a text file named Modelfile containing these two lines:

steps.title: Build the copy
steps.body: Run this in the folder that holds the Modelfile. It creates a model named local-64k. This much context needs a lot of memory: after your first message run ollama ps, and if PROCESSOR shows a CPU/GPU split, the model spilled out of your graphics card and will be slower.

steps.title: Point Hermes at Ollama
steps.body: Run hermes setup, choose Custom Endpoint, enter the base URL below, leave the API key empty (or type no-key) and set the model to local-64k. Or edit ~/.hermes/config.yaml (the .hermes folder in your home folder) to contain this. The Hermes guide also offers a setup wizard: run hermes setup, choose Custom Endpoint, and enter http://localhost:11434/v1 with no API key.

steps.title: If Hermes is on a different machine than Ollama
steps.body: Use the model computer's address instead of localhost in base_url (for example http://192.168.1.50:11434/v1), and set the Ollama computer's OLLAMA_HOST user environment variable to 0.0.0.0:11434, then restart Ollama. Hermes' guide does not cover this case; it is the standard Ollama setting. Only do it on a network you trust, and run the ollama create step on the computer that runs Ollama.

steps.title: Start it and be patient
steps.body: Hermes' guide warns that the first reply can take minutes while the model reads its instructions, and that a slow computer may need a longer timeout (HERMES_API_TIMEOUT=1800 in ~/.hermes/.env). If a reply shows raw JSON, tool calling is not working: use a model that lists the tools tag on its Ollama page. Run hermes doctor to diagnose setup problems.

files.name: SOUL.md
files.what: Its personality, tone and style. You write it. Loaded first in every session.

files.name: USER.md
files.what: Notes about you (role, preferences). The agent writes it with its memory tool; limit 1,375 characters.

files.name: MEMORY.md
files.what: The agent's own notes (environment facts, conventions, lessons). Limit 2,200 characters, so it holds about 8 to 15 entries.

files.name: AGENTS.md or .hermes.md
files.what: Project instructions. Only one project file loads: .hermes.md first, then AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules.

notes: Memory is loaded at the start of a session as a snapshot. What the agent saves mid-session is on disk at once but only appears in the prompt next session.
Memory does not shrink by itself: when it is full, writes fail until entries are shortened or removed. Consolidate when it is above 80 percent.
Older conversations are kept in a searchable database, so they do not need to be squeezed into memory.

- Windows machine, PowerShell. Python is started with: py
- Run the tests with: py -m pytest -q
- The model runs on another computer; do not try to start Ollama here.
- Ask before deleting files.

clients.name: Continue

steps.title: Add the model

clients.name: Cline
clients.blurb: An agent inside VS Code that reads your project, edits files and runs commands, asking you first.

steps.title: Install it
steps.body: Install the Cline extension in VS Code and make sure Ollama is running.

steps.title: Point it at Ollama
steps.body: In Cline's settings choose the provider Ollama, set the base URL to the address below, then pick {tag} from the model list (pull it first if it is missing).

steps.title: Turn on the compact prompt
steps.body: Cline Settings > Features > Use Compact Prompt. Cline's docs recommend this for local models: it makes the instructions Cline sends shorter, so small models cope better.

steps.title: Keep tasks small
steps.body: Start a new task when the conversation gets long. Local models slow down and lose track as the context fills.

files.name: Rules file
files.where: .clinerules/ in the project (or Cline's global custom instructions)
files.what: Instructions loaded for the project. The Memory Bank instructions go here.

files.name: memory-bank/
files.what: Plain Markdown files that carry the project between sessions: projectbrief.md, productContext.md, activeContext.md (current focus, updated most), systemPatterns.md, techContext.md, progress.md.

notes: To start: copy the Memory Bank instructions from Cline's doc into .clinerules/memory-bank.md, then tell Cline "initialize memory bank".
At a checkpoint say "update memory bank", start a new conversation, then say "follow your custom instructions" so it re-reads the files.
The Memory Bank is a lot of reading for a model with a small context window. With a local model, start with just projectbrief.md and activeContext.md (this is this page's advice, not Cline's).

clients.name: opencode
clients.blurb: An agent that runs in your terminal inside a project folder. You describe the job; it reads files, edits them and runs commands.

steps.title: Install it
steps.body: Any one of these works. On Windows the opencode docs recommend WSL (Windows' built-in Linux); native options are npm, Chocolatey and Scoop. Shortcut: Ollama's docs say you can skip the manual config below by running ollama launch opencode (add --config to only write the config). They also say OpenCode needs a context length of 64K or more.

steps.title: Tell it about your local model
steps.body: Create a file named opencode.json in your project folder with this content. The model name must match the Ollama tag exactly. The context number in 'limit' only helps opencode track usage: the real limit is the one Ollama is set to (next step).

steps.title: Set Ollama's context to match
steps.body: opencode's docs say that if tool calls fail, raise Ollama's num_ctx to about 16K to 32K. Use the 'Raise the context length' step above with {ctx}, then restart Ollama.

steps.title: Start it
steps.body: Go to your project folder, run opencode, and choose the {tag} model with /models. Run /init once if you want it to write an AGENTS.md summary of your project.

files.name: AGENTS.md (project)
files.what: Instructions added to the model's context for every session in that project. Commit it to Git.

files.name: AGENTS.md (global)
files.what: Your personal rules for all projects. Stays out of Git.

files.name: /init
files.what: Scans the repo and writes or improves AGENTS.md (build and test commands, layout, conventions).

files.name: instructions list
files.what: Extra files (globs or URLs) combined with AGENTS.md. If there is no AGENTS.md, opencode falls back to CLAUDE.md.

clients.name: LM Studio
clients.kind: Alternative to Ollama: an app with its own model catalog and chat window
clients.blurb: A desktop app (Mac, Windows, Linux) that downloads models, chats with them and can serve them to other tools. It does not use Ollama, so you do not need the Ollama steps above if you choose it.

steps.body: Search for the model inside the app's model download screen. clients.name: Goose
clients.kind: Coding and automation agent (terminal and desktop app)
clients.blurb: An open-source agent, now under the Linux Foundation, that runs tasks using tools and extensions. It leans heavily on tool calling.

steps.title: Install Goose
steps.body: Download it from the Goose docs site (link below). Its Ollama guide does not give an install command, so follow the install page there.

steps.title: Point it at Ollama

steps.title: Use a model that supports tool calling
steps.body: Goose's guide says models without tool calling can only chat, and you would have to switch off all Goose extensions. Check that the model's Ollama page shows the tools tag.

steps.title: Raise the context if extensions misbehave
steps.body: Goose's guide says that if it ignores extensions or its .goosehints file, the context is probably too small. Use the 'Raise the context length' step above with {ctx}.

clients.name: AnythingLLM
clients.blurb: A desktop app for asking questions of your own files. It stores the documents' search index itself and uses Ollama for the answers.

steps.title: Install it
steps.body: Install AnythingLLM from its website (its Ollama guide links to the download). Ollama must already be installed and running.

steps.title: Connect it to Ollama
steps.body: In AnythingLLM's LLM settings choose Ollama, and use this base URL. Then choose {tag} as the model. You can change the model later in Settings.

steps.title: Check the context
steps.body: AnythingLLM's Ollama guide does not say what context it needs. If answers ignore your documents, use the 'Raise the context length' step above with {ctx} and run ollama ps.

steps.body: A 2026 review (StorageReview) says telemetry is on by default and that an earlier code-execution flaw was fixed in version 1.11.2 or later. Use a current version and review its privacy settings.

clients.name: PocketPal AI
clients.kind: Phone app (Android and iPhone), open source
clients.blurb: A free app that runs models entirely on the phone, with no Ollama and no computer needed. It runs GGUF models with llama.cpp, and you add models from its built-in list or from Hugging Face.

steps.title: Install the app
steps.body: Install PocketPal AI from Google Play (or the App Store on an iPhone). Its README names only those two stores.

steps.title: Add the model
steps.body: {name} is our pick for this phone, but it is not in the app's built-in list (see the list below), so add it yourself: tap the + button, choose Hugging Face, and search for "{name}" plus GGUF. Choose a quantization (the number such as Q4) whose file is well under the memory figure above. If you would rather start with no searching, any model in the built-in list below works: tap Download.

steps.title: Load it and chat
steps.body: Press the model's load button, then open the chat and type. If the app closes or the phone gets hot, pick a smaller model or a smaller quantization.

steps.title: Measure it
steps.body: The app has a Benchmark page that reports tokens per second and memory used. Send me those numbers and they will replace the page's estimate for this phone.

clients.builtin_src: Read from the app's Models screen on the owner's phone, not from a published list. It may differ by version.

context_general.title: Get more from it: memory and context files
context_general.intro: These tools forget everything when a session ends, so the usual trick is a short file that is loaded at the start of every session. What you put in it, and how much, matters more with a small local model than with a big hosted one.
tips: Everything in an always-loaded file uses part of the model's context window, and a bigger context needs more memory and runs slower. Keep these files short: Hermes itself caps its memory file at 2,200 characters (about 800 tokens) for this reason.

Put what rarely changes (how to run the tests, where things live, rules you always repeat) in the project file. Put the current state of the work in a few lines you update, and start a fresh session at a natural break instead of letting one chat grow forever.

Write each rule as a short, concrete line (a command, a path, a yes or no) rather than a paragraph. This is a rule of thumb, not something from a tool's docs: smaller models tend to follow short, specific lines better than long prose.
Keep personal preferences (tone, your OS and shell) in the tool's global file and project facts in the project file, so a new project starts with your habits but not the old project's details.
Files are usually read when a session starts. After editing one, start a new session (Hermes states this outright for its files) and ask the model what it was told to check it was read.
Match Ollama's context length to the tool (64K for the agents), as in the steps above. A long context file with a 4K default context will simply be cut off.

tutorials.about: First-session walkthroughs for the tools. Only commands and behaviors from the tools' own docs are stated as fact; example prompts are written for this page and should be adjusted to your project. A step can show a real screenshot if you add a file named in its `shot` field to the screens/ folder (see README).

opencode.title: Your first session with opencode
opencode.intro: opencode runs in a terminal inside your project folder. You type what you want, it reads files, proposes or makes changes and can run commands.
opencode.first_task: Ask it to explain your project before you let it change anything.
prompts: Give me a quick summary of the codebase.
Switch to Plan, then: I want to add a dark mode toggle. List the files you would change and why. Do not edit anything yet.
In Build: make the change you described, then tell me how to test it.

walkthrough.title: Open your project
walkthrough.body: In a terminal, go into the project folder and start opencode. You can also pass the folder: opencode /path/to/project.

walkthrough.title: Check which model it is using
walkthrough.body: Type /models to list models and pick the local one you set up in opencode.json (the model name matches your Ollama tag).

walkthrough.title: Let it learn the project (once)
walkthrough.body: Run /init. It guides you through creating or updating an AGENTS.md file that describes the project to the agent. opencode's docs suggest committing that file to Git.

walkthrough.title: Start in Plan, not Build
walkthrough.body: Press Tab to cycle between its main agents. Build is the default and has all tools on (it can edit files and run commands). Plan is for analysis: it cannot edit your code (it may write its own plan notes). For anything you are not sure about, plan first, then Tab to Build.

walkthrough.title: Point at files and run commands
walkthrough.body: Type @ and start a file name to attach that file to your message. Start a message with ! to run a shell command and put its output into the conversation.

walkthrough.title: Undo if it goes wrong
walkthrough.body: /undo removes the last message, the replies after it and any file changes. /redo brings them back. Both need the project to be a Git repository, so run git init first if it is not.

commands.what: Switch between Build and Plan agents
List and switch models
Create or update AGENTS.md for the project
Remove or restore the last message and its file changes (needs Git)
Shrink the session so far to save context (useful with local models)
Start a fresh session
Switch between past sessions
Show help

careful: Build can edit files and run commands. Use a Git repository and commit before big jobs so /undo and Git can rescue you.
Local models have a short memory: if replies get worse in a long session, use /compact or /new, and check that Ollama's context is raised (the page's earlier step).

aider.title: Your first session with Aider
aider.intro: Aider works in a Git project. You tell it which files it may edit, ask for a change, and it edits the files and commits the result so you can undo it.
aider.first_task: Add one small file, ask a question about it, then ask for one small change.
prompts: Explain what this file does in plain language.
Add a function that checks whether a name is empty and use it in the form handler.
Write a test for the function you just added.

walkthrough.title: Start inside a Git repository
walkthrough.body: Go to your project and start Aider with your Ollama model. Naming files after the command adds them to the chat.
walkthrough.cmd:
cd path/to/your/project
aider --model ollama_chat/<tag from this page> src/app.js

walkthrough.title: Add only the files that need editing
walkthrough.body: Aider's docs say extra files can confuse the model and cost more tokens; Aider pulls related context from the rest of the repo by itself. Add files with /add.

walkthrough.title: Ask first, then change
walkthrough.body: A third-party Aider cheat sheet describes /ask (read-only questions, no edits) and /code (the normal editing mode), and suggests planning in /ask and then switching to /code. These commands come from that cheat sheet, not Aider's own usage page, so check them with /help.
walkthrough.cmd:
/ask Where is the form submitted?
/code Add the empty-name check.

walkthrough.title: Review what it did
walkthrough.body: Aider shows diffs of its changes and commits them to Git. /diff shows the last change.

walkthrough.title: Undo what you do not want
walkthrough.body: /undo reverts the last change Aider made.

walkthrough.title: Run your tests through Aider
walkthrough.body: From the same cheat sheet: /run runs a command and feeds the output back; /test runs your configured test command.

commands.what: Add a file so Aider can edit it
Undo Aider's last change
Switch models in the chat
Ask Aider how to use Aider
Chat modes: question only, normal editing, planner then editor (cheat sheet)
Show last change, run a command, run tests, remove files from the chat (cheat sheet)

careful: Aider commits for you. Start from a clean Git state so its commits are easy to spot and undo.
Ollama's default context is small and it silently drops what does not fit: raise it as in the earlier step.

cline.title: Your first session with Cline
cline.intro: Cline is a panel inside VS Code. It reads your project, proposes edits and commands, and waits for your approval before acting (unless you turn on auto-approve).
cline.first_task: Use Plan mode to have it explain how to make a change, read the plan, then switch to Act.
prompts: Plan: I want the settings page to remember the last tab. Which files are involved and what would you change?
Act: go ahead with the plan, one file at a time.

walkthrough.title: Open the project and the Cline panel
walkthrough.body: Open your project folder in VS Code, then open Cline from its icon. It should already point at Ollama from the setup steps.

walkthrough.title: Start in Plan mode
walkthrough.body: Plan mode lets Cline read your code, search and discuss approaches, but not change files or run commands. Cline's docs suggest: plan, discuss the approach, then switch to Act when you are confident. For tiny fixes (a typo) you can go straight to Act.

walkthrough.title: Approve each action
walkthrough.body: In Act mode Cline asks you before reading files, editing files or running commands, unless the matching auto-approve setting is on. Read what it proposes before clicking approve.

walkthrough.title: Set safe auto-approve
walkthrough.body: Cline's docs recommend allowing only reading project files at first and leaving edits, commands, browser and MCP off until you need them. If you allow edits, use Checkpoints so you can roll back. YOLO mode approves everything and the docs call it dangerous.

walkthrough.title: Big jobs
walkthrough.body: For large cross-cutting changes, Cline's docs point to the /deep-planning command. Keep the conversation short and start a new task when it gets long: local models slow down as the context fills.

commands.what: Plan: read and discuss only. Act: edit files and run commands (with your approval)
For large, multi-step changes (per Cline's docs)
Roll back after edits; turn on before Act

careful: Do not turn on YOLO mode with a local model. Small models make more mistakes and YOLO removes your chance to catch them.
Use Cline's compact prompt setting from the setup steps: it helps small models.

continue.title: Using Continue for as-you-type help
continue.intro: Continue shows grey suggestions as you type in VS Code or JetBrains. Press a key to accept one. It also has a chat panel.
continue.first_task: Turn on autocomplete, open a code file, and start writing a function.
prompts: Start typing a function name and a comment describing it, then pause and see what appears.
Select a function and ask in the chat panel: what does this do?

walkthrough.title: Turn autocomplete on
walkthrough.body: Click the Continue button in the bottom-right status bar of your editor, or tick Enable Tab Autocomplete in your editor's settings. Your autocomplete model needs the autocomplete role in config.yaml (see the setup steps).

walkthrough.title: Type and pause
walkthrough.body: Start writing code. A suggestion appears after a short pause.

walkthrough.title: Accept or reject
walkthrough.body: Tab accepts the whole suggestion. Esc rejects it. Ctrl/Cmd + Right arrow accepts one word at a time.
walkthrough.cmd: Tab = accept   Esc = reject   Ctrl/Cmd+Right = one word

walkthrough.title: Ask for a suggestion
walkthrough.body: In VS Code, Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + Space asks for a suggestion right now, even after you dismissed one.

walkthrough.title: Use chat for questions
walkthrough.body: Continue also has Chat, Edit, Agent and Plan modes. Its docs name the shortcuts Ctrl/Cmd+L and Ctrl/Cmd+I and @ for adding context, but the pages I could read did not say what each does, so open Continue's own docs for those.

commands.what: Accept the suggestion
Reject the suggestion
Accept one word of the suggestion
Ask for a suggestion now (VS Code)

careful: If suggestions are slow or never appear, the model is too big for your computer: use the small Qwen2.5-Coder this page recommends, not a large model.
Ollama unloads idle models after 5 minutes, so the first suggestion after a break can lag.

hermes.title: Your first session with Hermes Agent
hermes.intro: Hermes is a terminal agent. You chat with it, it uses tools (files, commands) to do jobs, and it asks before running dangerous commands.
hermes.first_task: Start a session, check it is using your local model, and give it one small, safe job.
prompts: List the files in this folder and tell me what this project is.
Create a file notes.md with a short summary of what you found. Show me before you run any command.
/bg Review the README for mistakes and give me a list (this runs in a separate background session)

walkthrough.title: Start it
walkthrough.body: hermes starts the classic interface. hermes --tui starts the modern text interface. Resume your last session later with hermes -c.

walkthrough.title: Check the model and context
walkthrough.body: /model shows or changes the model. /status shows session info. /context shows how much of the context window is used, which matters a lot with local models.

walkthrough.title: Give it a job
walkthrough.body: Type your request and press Enter. Alt+Enter, Ctrl+J or Shift+Enter add a new line. Start a line with ! to run a shell command yourself without asking the model, for example !git status.

walkthrough.title: Approvals
walkthrough.body: Commands that match dangerous patterns (such as rm -rf) go through an approval prompt. Hermes' CLI page does not describe a separate approval step for file edits (see its Security guide). Do not use --yolo or /yolo, which turns on auto-approve.

walkthrough.title: Interrupt or redirect
walkthrough.body: Ctrl+C on an empty prompt interrupts the agent (it clears a typed draft first). /stop cancels the turn. Typing and pressing Enter mid-turn redirects the agent by default.

walkthrough.title: Long jobs
walkthrough.body: /bg <prompt> runs a prompt in a separate background session. When the context bar is nearly full (95% or more), run /compress.

commands.what: Show or change the model
Session info, context-window use, usage and cost
List the tools Hermes can use
Run a prompt in a background session
Cancel the current turn
Shrink the context when the bar is nearly full
Name the session so you can resume it by name
Resume the latest session
Diagnose setup problems

careful: A first reply can take minutes on a slow computer while the model reads Hermes' instructions: wait before assuming it is stuck.
Hermes needs at least 64K context: if answers wander, check /context and that you are using the 64K copy of the model from the setup steps.

open-webui.title: Using Open WebUI, including chatting with your documents
open-webui.intro: Open WebUI is a chat page in your browser. You pick a model, chat, and can attach your own documents so the model answers from them.
open-webui.first_task: Chat once, then upload one document and ask a question about it.
prompts: Summarize the attached document in five bullet points.
According to the document, what are the deadlines?
Quote the part of the document that supports that answer.

walkthrough.title: Open it and pick the model
walkthrough.body: Go to the address from the setup (http://localhost:3000 for Docker) and choose your model at the top of a new chat.

walkthrough.title: Upload a document
walkthrough.body: Open Workspace, then Documents, and upload your file. (Open WebUI's docs also describe Knowledge collections under Workspace > Knowledge for groups of documents.)

walkthrough.title: Reference it in a chat
walkthrough.body: In a chat, type # and pick the document from the suggestions that appear above the message box. A document icon appears above the message box when it is attached. You can also start a prompt with # and a web address to bring in a web page.

walkthrough.title: Raise the context length
walkthrough.body: Open WebUI's docs warn that on graphics cards under 24 GB, Ollama's default context is 4096 tokens, which can leave retrieved text unused. In Settings > Admin > Models, click Edit on your model, open Advanced Params and raise the context length: at least 8192, and more than 16,000 is better for web pages.

walkthrough.title: If answers ignore your document
walkthrough.body: Check the context length above first. The docs also explain that knowledge attached to a model (rather than to the chat) depends on its function-calling setting; attaching the knowledge in the chat is the simplest fix.

commands.what: Reference an uploaded document or a web address
Upload files
Collections of documents you can attach

commands.cmd: Settings > Admin > Models > Edit > Advanced Params
commands.what: Raise the context length

careful: Models answer from what they retrieve, so check important facts against the document itself.
Complex files such as DOCX parse better in a normal chat than in Temporary Chat (per the docs).

os.about: Evidence behind the operating-system advice. Numbers are from the named sources and are reports, not measurements on your machines. The page's own calculation (how much memory a lighter OS would free and whether the recommendation changes) uses the page's fit model.

speed.text: Reports put native Linux about 5 to 25 percent faster than Windows for the same model and graphics card, with the gap larger for big or partly CPU-run models. The only direct comparison found says 22 percent faster (GPU not named); another review says there is no widely cited controlled study and calls 5 to 15 percent a rough consensus. For small models on a strong card the difference may not be noticeable.

wsl.text: Running Ollama inside WSL2 (Linux inside Windows) measured 10 to 13 percent slower than Ollama running directly on Windows in one 2024 test (RTX 4080, a 3B model, an old Ollama version). Another review says WSL2 is within a few percent of native Linux, and that WSL2 by default gets only half of your RAM unless you change .wslconfig.

vram.text: Windows' desktop uses roughly 200 to 500 MB of graphics-card memory (reported, not measured). That is marginal on a 24 GB card and matters on a 6 to 8 GB card.

ram.text: Idle memory use is reported at roughly 3.5 to 4 GB on Windows versus 0.3 to 0.5 GB for headless Linux (no method given; check Task Manager yourself). It matters most on machines that run models from system RAM.

nvidia.text: Ollama supports NVIDIA cards with compute capability 5.0 or higher and driver 550 or newer on both Windows and Linux: RTX 20, 30, 40 and 50 series are supported.

amd.text: Ollama's AMD support differs by system: on Windows it covers only the RX 7000 series and Radeon PRO W7500 to W7900; on Linux it also covers RX 6000 and 9000 series and more. If you have an AMD card, Linux gives you more chance of GPU use.

apple.text: On Apple silicon Ollama uses the Mac's graphics (Metal) and the unified memory, so macOS is the platform to use.

server.text: For a machine that runs the model all the time for other computers, one review recommends Linux, which avoids forced updates and leaves more memory for the model.

power.text: No reliable evidence that Linux uses less power. Forum readings go both ways and mostly trace to drivers and settings: one user's RTX 3090 drew about 110 W at the Windows desktop until a clean driver reinstall (about 190 W total fell to about 80 W), while others report NVIDIA cards drawing more on Linux (about 27 W vs 9 W when browsing on a GTX 1660 Ti). These are single-machine reports, not controlled tests.

server_win.text: On Windows, updates restart the PC by themselves outside 'active hours' (default 8 AM to 5 PM, at most 18 hours long), and the setting that blocks restarts while someone is signed in is one Microsoft says can mean updates never finish. Ollama on Windows starts when you sign in, not when the PC boots, so after an automatic restart it will not serve other computers until someone signs in (or the PC signs in automatically).

server_net.text: By default Ollama listens only on the computer itself (127.0.0.1). To let other computers use it, set OLLAMA_HOST to 0.0.0.0:11434 on the serving machine (on Windows: quit Ollama, edit your account's environment variables, start Ollama again).
